h: A guillotine, a clock with a show and Scotland's oldest treasures
p: A few objects here have a way of sticking in the memory. The Maiden is an early Scottish beheading machine used in Edinburgh centuries before the French Revolution made the guillotine famous, and it's every bit as grim and fascinating as it sounds. Nearby, the tiny Monymusk Reliquary is a beautifully decorated early medieval container thought to have carried relics of a saint into battle.

In the Grand Gallery, keep an eye on the Millennium Clock, a towering, quirky sculpture packed with carved figures and moving parts. When it springs into life it's a bit of a spectacle, and children love waiting for it. The natural world galleries are home to a cast of a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton and a huge array of animals, which tends to be the point where younger visitors refuse to move on.

If your family likes to get hands on, the science and technology areas have plenty of buttons, puzzles and gadgets. For a calmer stretch, the Scottish history floors build up slowly from early peoples through medieval kingdoms, the Jacobites and industry, so you can pick your era and dive in.

Allow at least two to three hours for a decent first look. It's a good idea to pick up a map and decide on a few must-sees before you start. Afterwards, you're perfectly placed for more Old Town exploring: the little statue of Greyfriars Bobby is just across the road, and Surgeons' Hall Museums on Nicolson Street are a few minutes away for anyone who likes their history a little gruesome.
